content: Dock9, also referred to as Zizimin1, is a large protein with a molecular weight of approximately 230 kDa. It plays a critical role in intracellular signaling pathways. Dock9 belongs to the DOCK-D subfamily within the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are known to activate small G proteins. Specifically, Dock9 functions as an activator of the small G protein Cdc42. Dock9 was initially identified through an affinity proteomic approach aimed at discovering novel activators of Cdc42 in fibroblasts. Subsequent northern blot analyses demonstrated that Dock9 is predominantly expressed in the brain, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, placenta, and lung. Lower levels of expression were observed in the colon, thymus, liver, small intestine, and peripheral blood leukocytes. Structurally, Dock9 shares two core domains, DHR1 and DHR2, which are characteristic of all members of the DOCK family. The C-terminal DHR2 domain serves as an atypical GEF domain for small G proteins, while the DHR1 domain, in certain DOCK-A/B/C subfamily proteins, facilitates recruitment to the plasma membrane. Unlike DOCK-A/B/C proteins, DOCK-D proteins, including Dock9, possess an N-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain that mediates their recruitment to the membrane. Dock9, along with other members of the DOCK-C/D subfamily, can activate Cdc42 both in vitro and in vivo through its DHR2 domain. However, Dock9 exists in an autoinhibitory conformation under resting conditions, which conceals the DHR2 domain. The precise mechanism by which this autoinhibition is relieved remains unclear. In other DOCK proteins that exhibit similar autoinhibition, activation often requires interaction with adaptor proteins such as ELMO. Additionally, Dock9 has been reported to form dimers under resting conditions via its DHR2 domains. This observation suggests that other DOCK family proteins may also dimerize in a similar manner. Recent studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the Dock9 gene that are associated with an increased risk and severity of bipolar disorder, highlighting its potential role in the pathophysiology of this condition.
